    Home/Learn/Peptides for libido: Vyleesi, Melanotan II and the rest

    Peptides for libido: what is approved, and what is not.

    Peptide Chooser editorial team. Checked 30 Oct 2026.

    Short answer

    Bremelanotide (Vyleesi) is FDA approved for premenopausal women with low sexual desire that causes distress and has no other cause.1 PT-141 is the same molecule, bremelanotide, sold by research-use shops without a prescription; that is not the approved product.23 Melanotan II is not approved for any use.3

    Which peptides are sold for libido?

    Our libido page lists three:

    • Bremelanotide (Vyleesi): FDA approved. A shot you take before sex, approved for low sexual desire in premenopausal women.
    • Sildenafil (Viagra): FDA approved. A pill taken about an hour before sex. It helps erections and works only with sexual stimulation.
    • Tadalafil (Cialis): FDA approved. A pill taken before sex, or at a lower dose once a day. It helps erections and works only with sexual stimulation.
    • Testosterone (TRT): FDA approved. Replaces a hormone the body makes too little of. Not FDA approved for low testosterone without an associated medical condition.
    • Enclomiphene: Not FDA approved; pharmacy-made. A pill some clinics prescribe for low testosterone. It is not FDA approved for any use, so only pharmacies make it.
    • Compounded tadalafil and PT-141: Not FDA approved; pharmacy-made. Pharmacy-made versions sold by online clinics, some mixed with other medicines. Not checked by the FDA batch by batch.
    • PT-141 from online shops: Not an approved product. The same molecule as Vyleesi, sold without a prescription by research-use shops: no dose control, no checks.
    • Melanotan II: Not approved for any use. A tanning peptide also sold "for libido". Linked to serious side effects; never approved anywhere.
    • Flibanserin (Addyi): FDA approved. Approved for acquired, generalized low sexual desire (HSDD) in women under 65 that is not caused by another condition, the relationship or a medicine. Not approved for men.

    What is Vyleesi approved for?

    Bremelanotide, sold as Vyleesi, is approved for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder: low sexual desire that causes marked distress or trouble in the relationship, and is not caused by another medical or mental health condition, problems in the relationship or a medicine.1

    It is not approved for men, for women after menopause or to boost desire in people without that condition.1

    What did the trials find?

    Two identical trials gave 1,267 premenopausal women bremelanotide or a placebo for 24 weeks, without them knowing which. Women on bremelanotide reported a small but clear rise in desire and less distress about low desire than women on the placebo.4

    More of them had nausea, flushing and headache: each came up in 10% or more of the women on bremelanotide in both trials.4 The trials were paid for by the companies that make it.4

    What does the Vyleesi label warn about?

    • Blood pressure rises for a short time and heart rate drops after each dose, usually for less than 12 hours. It is not for people with uncontrolled high blood pressure or known heart disease.1
    • Nausea is common: 40% of patients in the studies reported it.1
    • About 1% had dark patches on the skin, for example on the face or gums, and in some they did not go away.1

    A prescriber checks these before and during treatment. A shop vial comes with none of that.

    Is PT-141 the same as Vyleesi?

    The molecule is the same: PT-141 was the research name of bremelanotide.2 The product is not. A PT-141 vial from a research-use shop is not the approved medicine: nobody checked how it was made, how much is in it or whether it is clean, and it comes without a prescriber.5

    What about Melanotan II?

    Melanotan II is a tanning peptide that is also sold for libido. It is not approved for any use.3

    The FDA says it may set off an immune reaction when given some ways, and that published case reports describe serious side effects, including melanoma, a brain swelling syndrome, an overdose-like reaction and painful erections that do not go away.6

    What do they cost?

    We show shop prices once the shops are in our database. The shop listings are research-use vials, not Vyleesi.

    The windows on our libido page list each shop with its five checks, and each name opens our page on that shop. A price per mg says nothing about what is in the vial.

    So which peptide works for libido?

    Only one has trials in people and FDA approval: bremelanotide as Vyleesi, for one group of women with one condition.1 The same molecule from a shop is a different product, and Melanotan II has serious case reports behind it and no approval.

    If low desire troubles you, a doctor can first look for the causes the Vyleesi label rules out: another health problem, the relationship or a medicine you take.1

    None of this is medical advice. A doctor can tell you what fits you.
